rows: Dengue is a viral infection transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes.
Illness can range from asymptomatic infection to severe disease.
Common features include fever, headache and muscle or joint pain.
Some patients develop warning signs requiring urgent clinical review.
Travel history and timing are important for diagnosis.
Clinical management includes careful assessment of hydration and deterioration.
Prevention relies on mosquito-bite avoidance in affected areas.
Fever after tropical travel does not establish dengue.
Conclusions require destination, timing, symptoms, laboratory, clinical course and alternative-diagnosis evidence.
Zika virus is transmitted mainly by Aedes mosquitoes.
Many infections cause no symptoms or only mild illness.
Infection during pregnancy can cause serious fetal effects.
Travel and pregnancy status are central to risk assessment.
Laboratory testing is available in defined circumstances.
Mosquito-bite and sexual-transmission precautions reduce risk.
Advice should use current country-risk and return-travel guidance.
Travel to a risk area or a mild rash does not establish Zika infection.
Conclusions require destination, timing, pregnancy, symptoms, exposure, testing and current guidance.
Food additives require authorisation for use in Great Britain.
The official register is the primary source for authorised food additives.
Register entries identify the substance and relevant conditions of use.
Food categories and maximum levels can limit an authorisation.
Specifications can define purity and identity requirements.
Businesses should confirm that the exact additive and use are covered.
Labelling should identify additives as required by food-information rules.
Changes to authorisation status should be checked against the current register.
An E number or supplier statement does not prove that an additive is authorised for a particular food and level.
Conclusions require identity, food category, function, level, specification, authorisation and label evidence.
Food flavourings are subject to authorisation and conditions of use.
The FSA register is the primary source for flavourings authorised in Great Britain.
Individual entries identify authorised substances and relevant details.
Conditions can restrict food categories or use levels.
Flavouring identity should match the authorised entry.
Businesses should check notes and additional conditions on product pages.
Labelling and business-to-business information requirements may apply.
The current register should be checked before use or reformulation.
A flavouring name or certificate of analysis does not prove authorisation for a specific application.
Conclusions require identity, category, level, conditions, formulation, authorisation and label evidence.
